messages.text: What is this paper about and what did they find?

messages.short_answer: PromptScaffold is a prompt editor that guides non-expert users through four template slots (role, task, examples, output format). In a 16-person within-subjects lab study, prompts written with it scored higher on three predefined tasks (mean 0.74 vs. 0.61) and users reported higher confidence, but they took longer and the evidence is limited to a small, homogeneous sample.

sections.title: What the study compared and found
sections.text: The authors compared free-form prompting in a plain text box with PromptScaffold, with three predefined tasks in each condition (sentiment classification, topic labelling, and two-sentence news summaries). The overview summary reports that the template prompts scored higher, with the largest gain on topic labelling, that confidence was higher (4.1 vs. 3.4 on a 7-point scale), and that the template took slightly longer (7.5 vs. 6.2 minutes).

sections.title: Where the template helped and where it constrained users
sections.text: According to the discussion, the template mainly helped by prompting participants to give examples and state the output format, which free-form prompts often lacked. However, it did not teach participants why these parts mattered, and several filled the slots mechanically. The overview also reports that some participants found the role slot artificial and felt the template made simple prompts long.

sections.title: Limits of the evidence
sections.text: The authors note a small, homogeneous sample of university students, a single 70-minute session, three tasks, one LLM, and only automatic and self-reported measures. The overview also flags that the results section cites an external study with n = 412 to claim effects across age groups and non-university participants, which the paper's own sample does not support.

sections.title: Possible relevance to your user study
sections.text: For your study of how non-expert users write prompts, the paper's slot structure could serve as a coding scheme for analysing prompt content, not only task scores. Its limits (homogeneous sample, self-report confidence, no expert ratings) suggest that your study might add more diverse participants and direct prompt-quality measures. You would need to decide whether these fit your research questions.

sources.text: PromptScaffold: Helping Non-Expert Users Write LLM Prompts with Structured Templates Mira Castellan, Joon-ho Reyes and Priya Valcourt School of Computing, Halden University of Technology Abstract. People without training in machine learning increasingly write prompts for large language model (LLM) tools, but often struggle to state the task, give examples and specify the output format. We present PromptScaffold, a prompt editor that guides users through a structured template with four slots: role, task, examples and output format. In a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants who completed three predefined tasks, prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher automatic task score than free-form prompts (mean 0.74 vs. 0.61) and participants reported higher confidence. We discuss what the template helped with, where it constrained participants, and the limits of a single short lab study. 1 Introduction LLM-based tools let anyone describe a task in natural language, yet writing an effective prompt remains difficult for people without machine-learning experience.
quotes: In a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants who completed three predefined tasks, prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher automatic task score than free-form prompts (mean 0.74 vs. 0.61) and participants reported higher confidence.

sources.text: Design and tasks. The study used a within-subjects design with two conditions: free-form prompting in a plain text box, and PromptScaffold. Each participant completed three predefined tasks in each condition: classifying customer reviews by sentiment, labelling support tickets by topic, and summarising short news articles in two sentences. Condition order was counterbalanced, and parallel task versions were used so that no participant saw the same inputs twice. All prompts were run on one LLM with fixed settings. Procedure and measures. Each session lasted about 70 minutes in our lab. The main outcome was an automatic task score between 0 and 1: accuracy against gold labels for the two classification tasks and a reference-based overlap score for summaries. After each condition, participants rated their confidence in their prompts on a 7-point scale. We also recorded the time to the final prompt and held a short interview at the end of the session. 5 Results Prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher task score than free-form prompts (Table 1). The difference was largest for the topic-labelling task, where the examples slot led most participants to add labelled examples.

sources.text: The paper introduces PromptScaffold, a prompt editor that guides users through four template slots: role, task, examples and output format. In a within-subjects lab study with 16 non-expert university students, prompts written with the template scored higher on three predefined tasks (mean 0.74 vs. 0.61) and gave higher self-rated confidence (4.1 vs. 3.4 on a 7-point scale). Participants needed more time (7.5 vs. 6.2 minutes), and interviews found the examples slot most useful, while some felt the role slot was artificial or that the template made simple prompts long. The authors note limitations: a small homogeneous sample, a single short session, three tasks, one LLM, and only automatic and self-reported measures. The results section also cites an external study with n = 412 to claim the effect held across age groups and for participants without university education, a claim that is not supported by the paper's own sample.

6 Discussion The template mainly helped by prompting participants to give examples and to state the output format, which free-form prompts often lacked. It did not teach participants why these parts mattered: several filled the slots mechanically. Designers of prompt tools for non-experts may therefore want to explain the purpose of each slot and let users drop slots that do not fit the task. 7 Limitations Our findings have three main limitations. First, the sample was small and homogeneous: 16 university students, most of them from computing courses, so the results may not hold for older users or for people outside a university. Second, each participant used PromptScaffold in a single 70-minute lab session; we did not study long-term or real-world use, and novelty may have raised confidence. Third, we used only three predefined classification and summarisation tasks and one LLM, and measured success only with an automatic task score and self-reported confidence. Open-ended tasks, other models and expert ratings of prompt quality may give different results.

1 Introduction LLM-based tools let anyone describe a task in natural language, yet writing an effective prompt remains difficult for people without machine-learning experience. Prior studies report that non-expert users tend to give instructions that are too short, rarely include examples, and leave the output format implicit. They then struggle to tell whether a poor result comes from the prompt or from the model. Structured templates are a common answer in practice, but there is little evidence on whether they help nonexperts write better prompts or only make prompts longer. This paper asks two questions. RQ1: Do prompts written with a structured template perform better on predefined tasks than free-form prompts? RQ2: How do non-expert users experience writing prompts with a template? We contribute (1) PromptScaffold, a template-based prompt editor; (2) a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants; and (3) observations on where templates help and where they constrain users. 2 Related Work Work on end-user programming shows that novices benefit from scaffolds that make implicit requirements explicit, such as forms and worked examples.

6 Discussion The template mainly helped by prompting participants to give examples and to state the output format, which free-form prompts often lacked. It did not teach participants why these parts mattered: several filled the slots mechanically. Designers of prompt tools for non-experts may therefore want to explain the purpose of each slot and let users drop slots that do not fit the task. 7 Limitations Our findings have three main limitations. First, the sample was small and homogeneous: 16 university students, most of them from computing courses, so the results may not hold for older users or for people outside a university. Second, each participant used PromptScaffold in a single 70-minute lab session; we did not study long-term or real-world use, and novelty may have raised confidence. Third, we used only three predefined classification and summarisation tasks and one LLM, and measured success only with an automatic task score and self-reported confidence. Open-ended tasks, other models and expert ratings of prompt quality may give different results.

2 Related Work Work on end-user programming shows that novices benefit from scaffolds that make implicit requirements explicit, such as forms and worked examples. Studies of prompt writing describe non-experts as relying on trial and error and on conversational phrasing. Prompt libraries and prompt-pattern catalogues offer reusable structures, but they are usually written for developers and have rarely been evaluated with non-expert users in a controlled setting. 3 The PromptScaffold Editor PromptScaffold splits a prompt into four slots. The role slot states who the model should act as. The task slot describes what to do, with a hint to name the input and the goal. The examples slot asks for one to three inputoutput pairs, and the output format slot asks how the answer should be structured. Each slot shows a short hint and an example. The editor assembles the slots into one prompt that the user can preview and edit freely before running it. A side panel shows the model's output for a small set of test inputs that the user provides. 4 Study Participants. We recruited 16 participants (9 women, 7 men, aged 19 to 27) through university mailing lists.

8 Conclusion PromptScaffold's structured template improved task scores and confidence for non-expert users on three predefined tasks in a short lab study. Future work should test the template with more diverse users, over longer periods and on open-ended tasks, and should examine how to explain the purpose of each slot.

Design and tasks. The study used a within-subjects design with two conditions: free-form prompting in a plain text box, and PromptScaffold. Each participant completed three predefined tasks in each condition: classifying customer reviews by sentiment, labelling support tickets by topic, and summarising short news articles in two sentences. Condition order was counterbalanced, and parallel task versions were used so that no participant saw the same inputs twice. All prompts were run on one LLM with fixed settings. Procedure and measures. Each session lasted about 70 minutes in our lab. The main outcome was an automatic task score between 0 and 1: accuracy against gold labels for the two classification tasks and a reference-based overlap score for summaries. After each condition, participants rated their confidence in their prompts on a 7-point scale. We also recorded the time to the final prompt and held a short interview at the end of the session. 5 Results Prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher task score than free-form prompts (Table 1). The difference was largest for the topic-labelling task, where the examples slot led most participants to add labelled examples.
